title: Cooperative exploration and target search
role: Graduate Researcher · Advisor: Dr. Srikanth Saripalli
summary: Cooperative exploration and object search with a Husky and two Jackals, integrating probabilistic localization, frontier-based task allocation, and visual perception.
challenge: I investigate how a robot team should divide its search as an unfamiliar environment is revealed. The work connects local state estimation and shared mapping to decisions about which robot explores each region.
contributions: Probabilistic localization

Fused odometry and inertial measurement unit (IMU) data with an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF), using prediction, covariance propagation, and measurement correction for local state estimation. Combined LiDAR observations in a shared occupancy map.
Frontier search and assignment

Implemented a Wavefront Frontier Detector (WFD) to group boundaries between known and unknown space. Used balanced Hungarian (Kuhn–Munkres) assignment with Euclidean travel-cost estimates and per-robot task capacities to distribute exploration.
Planning and control
Combined cost-aware A* global planning with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control. This couples map-based route search with sampled local motion, while the coordinator handles reassignment.
Visual target detection
Integrated pretrained YOLO inference through PyTorch/CUDA, using confirmation across successive frames to report target detections during exploration.
outcome: My ongoing research extends geometric exploration toward capability-aware allocation and semantic viewpoint selection: choosing where to search based on robot mobility and the information a scene may provide.
imageAlt: Exploration workflow: EKF localization supports shared LiDAR mapping, wavefront frontier detection, Hungarian task allocation, and A* planning and MPPI control. Camera-based target detection runs alongside exploration.
imageCaption: Shared mapping and task allocation coordinate exploration while visual detection identifies the target.

title: Perception and planning for rural roads
eyebrow: Autonomous Vehicles for All · Perception & planning
role: Graduate Research Assistant · Advisor: Dr. Reza Langari
summary: Road perception, Frenet-frame trajectory planning, and visual-representation analysis for autonomous driving in environments with weak lane markings and unreliable visibility.
imageAlt: Annotated AVA research vehicle with its sensor locations
imageCaption: AVA research vehicle and sensor layout. My work focused on perception and motion planning.
challenge: My work in Autonomous Vehicles for All examined how uncertain road boundaries affect trajectory selection. A complementary study explored redundancy in the visual inputs of a vision-language-action (VLA) driving model.
contributions: Road-relative trajectory planning

Developed a Frenet-frame planner that separates progress along the road from lateral displacement. Generated candidate offsets and speed profiles, then selected trajectories using curvature constraints and a weighted cost function.
Perception and sensor alignment
Tuned CLRerNet lane detection and Segment Anything Model (SAM) drivable-area masks. Aligned camera, LiDAR, and odometry data in a common frame to connect road-boundary estimates with planning.
Sensitivity to degraded inputs
Examined glare, low light, dust, sensor dropout, and timing jitter using recorded ROS data and simulation. Refined detection thresholds and temporal smoothing to maintain lane continuity.
Visual representation analysis

Applied Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to OpenDriveVLA features from 6,019 nuScenes samples. About 10 components retained 80% of scene-token variance and 97% of map-token variance, revealing a compact representation for further token-reduction studies.
outcome: This work connected perception quality to feasible motion and identified visual redundancy relevant to more efficient VLA inference.

title: Precision Vehicle Tracking and Disturbance Recovery
date: 2024 concept study · 2026 tracking and recovery study
summary: Reference-scheduled Linear Parameter-Varying Model Predictive Control (LPV-MPC) for recovering from tracking errors and temporary disturbances while respecting steering, acceleration, and command-rate limits.
challenge: I investigated how a predictive controller recovers from initial misalignment and an unmodeled disturbance while following a changing reference trajectory. The study examines tracking accuracy and command smoothness under explicit input limits.
contributions: Prediction model
Formulated along-track, cross-track, heading, and speed errors about a time-indexed reference. Scheduled a local linear model by reference speed and curvature over a 20-step horizon.
Constrained optimization

Assembled a sparse quadratic program (QP) and solved it with OSQP, an operator-splitting solver. Applied the first command and replanned every 100 ms of simulated time, with steering, acceleration, rate, and speed bounds.
Recovery evaluation

Evaluated variable-speed oval, figure-eight, and disturbed lane-change trajectories using a nonlinear kinematic bicycle model with fourth-order Runge–Kutta (RK4) integration. Measured full-run tracking errors and post-disturbance recovery, with independent checks on command, rate, and sampled-speed limits.
outcome: All 1,520 QP solves succeeded and the configured command, rate, and sampled-speed checks passed. Full-run position root mean square error (RMSE) ranged from 0.289 to 0.396 m, including startup recovery.
resources: Precision Vehicle Tracking and Disturbance Recovery · theoretical report
sourceNote: Builds on concepts from Mark Misin’s study.

title: Robotic welding automation
role: Graduate Research Assistant · Advisor: Dr. Prabhakar Pagilla
summary: CAD-guided robotic welding that combines rigid registration, constrained manipulator motion, and weld-pool feedback on a UR10e and Miller pulsed-MIG platform.
challenge: My research connected the geometry of a planned weld to its execution on a physical workpiece. I developed methods for workpiece alignment, continuous torch motion, and feedback regulation of welding conditions.
contributions: Rigid registration

Aligned three torch-probed points with the CAD model using the Kabsch algorithm, followed by Iterative Closest Point (ICP) refinement. This establishes the workpiece-to-robot transformation without external metrology.
Manipulator planning

Generated weld paths from STL edges and surface normals. Combined Newton–Raphson inverse kinematics (IK) with Rapidly-exploring Random Tree star (RRT*) planning, wrist-limit handling, and angle unwrapping to construct continuous joint trajectories.
Coordinated execution

Time-parameterized motion for approximately constant torch-tip speed and synchronized weld triggering with approach and retreat. Integrated planning, visualization, and welder commands in a Python/PyQt5/ROS interface.
Process feedback

Integrated Optris PI 05M infrared monitoring and used bead-height and calibrated temperature feedback to regulate travel speed and arc voltage, linking the observed weld-pool state to process commands.
outcome: The resulting workflow connects CAD geometry, robot motion, and welding-process feedback within one system, bringing geometric planning and process regulation together.

title: Robot motion and feedback control at MIKO
summary: Model-based motion and feedback control for interactive robots, spanning expressive articulation, self-balancing mobility, and audio-directed orientation.
challenge: At MIKO, I worked on the connection between robot dynamics and interactive behavior. My role combined system identification, controller synthesis, sensor integration, and hardware experiments across several motion-control problems.
contributions: System identification and articulation
Used measured mechanism responses to inform dynamic models and robust controller design for a head-motion manipulator. Developed path-planning and control software for expressive joint motion.
Balance control
Integrated the sensor suite of a self-balancing robot and tuned feedback controllers to regulate balance. Evaluated stability and motion on the physical platform.
Perception-driven orientation
Mapped audio direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimates to yaw-axis control, enabling the robot to face an active speaker. Added remote-control functionality for the mobile platform.
outcome: This work carried control methods through modeling, implementation, and hardware testing, connecting stability and tracking requirements to expressive robot behavior.
sourceNote: The demonstration shows a self-balancing prototype, not a specific commercial MIKO product.

title: Robust control for vehicle platooning
summary: Robust longitudinal and lateral control of a three-vehicle platoon, examining how sliding-mode formulations trade tracking accuracy against control effort.
imageAlt: Master's thesis plot of lateral tracking error using super-twisting control
imageCaption: Lateral tracking error with super-twisting control, reproduced from my master's thesis.
challenge: My master’s research addressed spacing regulation and path following under nonlinear vehicle dynamics. I compared controller behavior through convergence, overshoot, tracking-error integrals, and control energy.
contributions: Dynamics and estimation
Modeled a three-vehicle platoon in MATLAB/Simulink at a reference speed of 8 m/s. Used a Luenberger observer to estimate yaw rate from lateral velocity for lateral control.
Nonlinear control

Compared proportional–integral–derivative (PID) control, conventional Sliding Mode Control (SMC), SMC with a Power Rate Exponential Reaching Law (PREL), and second-order super-twisting control for both motion channels.
Comparative analysis
Compared integral absolute and squared errors (IAE/ISE), their time-weighted forms, and control energy across all three vehicles to distinguish tracking accuracy from actuation effort.
outcome: PREL-based SMC produced the lowest error indices in the simulation comparison. Super-twisting achieved lateral convergence without overshoot and the lowest longitudinal control energy. Related work was presented at ACODS 2022.

title: A robot swarm searching for light
summary: Cooperative light-source search with three mobile robots, using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to turn individual measurements into a shared search strategy.
imageAlt: LEGO NXT robot carrying an ArUco tracking marker
imageCaption: LEGO NXT platform with an ArUco marker for overhead tracking.
challenge: I investigated how local measurements can guide collective search when the brightest location is unknown. The project translated a population-based optimization method into coordinated movement on three LEGO NXT robots.
contributions: Collective search

Represented each robot as a PSO particle, combining its personal-best light observation with the global best found by the swarm. Developed the search in MATLAB and implemented the hardware workflow in Python.
Visual localization
Tracked the robots with an overhead camera and ArUco fiducial markers. Supplied position feedback to a centralized controller communicating with the robots over Bluetooth.
Navigation and sensing
Integrated light measurements, waypoint following, and ultrasonic obstacle avoidance so the robots could pursue search locations around static obstacles and one another.
outcome: The robots converged on the brightest region in the arena; one documented trial required 11 iterations. The related paper received a Best Paper Award at ICECA 2019.

title: EKF-SLAM and embedded robot navigation
eyebrow: IIT Bombay internship · Estimation & embedded control
role: Summer intern · Joint project with Alden J. Joseph
summary: Extended Kalman Filter–based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (EKF-SLAM) for joint pose and landmark estimation, alongside embedded mobile-robot navigation.
imageAlt: MATLAB EKF-SLAM simulation showing a robot path and landmark estimates
imageCaption: EKF-SLAM simulation from the internship report, showing a waypoint route and estimated landmarks.
challenge: I studied how motion and measurement uncertainty affect a robot’s estimate of its position and surroundings. The internship paired a probabilistic mapping study in MATLAB with a separate navigation implementation on a SPARK-V robot.
contributions: Joint state estimation

Adapted an EKF-SLAM simulator to estimate robot pose and landmark positions together. Used Jacobian linearization to propagate uncertainty through the joint state covariance during prediction and measurement updates.
Landmark association

Used uncertainty-aware nearest-neighbor association with Mahalanobis gating to match range–bearing measurements to existing landmarks and identify new features. Examined how repeated observations reduced landmark uncertainty.
Reactive and embedded navigation
Extended the simulator with reactive steering from three sensor views. Programmed ultrasonic obstacle avoidance and wheel-encoder distance feedback in Embedded C on the SPARK-V’s ATmega16 controller.
outcome: Waypoint revisits reduced map uncertainty in the MATLAB study. The SPARK-V demonstrated room traversal using obstacle avoidance and encoder feedback, connecting estimation concepts with practical sensing and control.

title: Needle-tip tracking with Kalman filtering
summary: Ultrasound needle-tip tracking that combines robust geometric fitting with recursive state estimation to reduce the effect of speckle and unreliable image features.
challenge: I investigated how temporal estimation can improve needle tracking when ultrasound images provide uncertain measurements. The approach combines image-derived needle geometry with a Kalman filter to update the tip estimate across frames.
contributions: Robust feature extraction

Built a LabVIEW pipeline with background subtraction and edge detection. Applied Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) line fitting within a region of interest to estimate needle geometry despite outlying image features.
Recursive estimation
Used a four-state Kalman Filter (KF) to combine predicted state with image measurements, maintaining a temporal estimate when speckle obscured the needle tip.
Experimental comparison
Compared tracking against an NDI-Aurora electromagnetic reference in artificial and biological tissue, at insertion depths up to 6.5 cm.
outcome: Relative to vision-only tracking, position root mean square error (RMSE) decreased from 0.79 to 0.03 cm in artificial tissue and from 0.84 to 0.21 cm in biological tissue.
